name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,731

clue.text: House too clean

blocks.note: HO is the standard abbreviation for house
too much is over the top, as in overcooked

explanation.surface: A complaint that someone keeps their home almost clinically tidy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House too clean' reads as one remark about a spotless home, but 'clean' alone is the definition, a verb. Hoover is a vacuum-cleaner brand, used in Britain as an everyday verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoover a carpet is to vacuum it, a common British verb for cleaning floors taken from the brand name.

clue.text: Arab wanting limits for female lives

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the phrase loses its outer edges at both ends

blocks.note: a female person
to live is to be, so lives gives is

explanation.surface: A man from the Arab world who must live without boundaries for women.
explanation.walkthrough: WOMAN IS loses its first and last letters, leaving OMANI.
explanation.definitionFit: An Omani is a native of Oman, a country on the Arabian peninsula, so a type of Arab.

clue.text: Love cafe back on descent when cycling up? U-turn

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept
in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the order runs backwards
a cycle goes round, so letters taken off one end come round to the other

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the final letter of descent

explanation.surface: A cyclist who loved a cafe at the foot of a hill turns round and pedals back up to it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'up' means read from the bottom; cycling then moves a block of letters from the end round to the front. Volte-face is borrowed from French and Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: A volte-face is a complete reversal of opinion or policy, figuratively the same as doing a U-turn.

clue.text: English judge with official outfit on is cool

blocks.note: a referee, the match official
a rig is a set of clothes or equipment
standard abbreviation
to rate is to assess or judge

explanation.surface: An English judge looks cool wearing his official robes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' in a down entry means above, so the official's outfit sits on top of the English judge: the two halves appear in the reverse of the clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: To refrigerate food is to chill it, lowering its temperature to keep it fresh; cool is a looser synonym.

clue.text: Recording full of American sailor's sweet accompaniment

indicators.note: something full of other things holds them inside its walls

blocks.note: a compact disc
standard abbreviation
tar is old slang for a sailor; the 's is a possessive link

explanation.surface: A record crammed with a US sailor's sugary backing track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accompaniment' suggests music for the recording, but it is a sauce. Custard, a sweet yellow sauce, is poured over British puddings.
explanation.definitionFit: Custard is the classic sauce served alongside desserts such as apple crumble, so it accompanies sweet courses.

clue.text: During tournament, miss shot from short range

indicators.note: something happening during an event sits within its span

blocks.note: a cup competition
to miss something is to lose it

explanation.surface: A sports report: in a tournament a player misses an easy shot from close in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like a sporting strike, but it is a camera shot.
explanation.definitionFit: A close-up is a photograph or film frame taken very near the subject, filling the picture.

clue.text: A day on the throne, perhaps

definitions.note: a verb, past tense: 'sat on the throne'

blocks.note: first meaning: the short form of Saturday
second meaning: was seated, as a monarch might be

explanation.surface: A single day of reigning, as if someone were king for a day.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a brief reign; the first two words are a day of the week abbreviated, the rest describes being seated.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturday is abbreviated in calendars, and a monarch who was seated on the throne is one who did that.

clue.text: Frame is lighter without fellow on top

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is dropped from the word
on top points to the head of the word, so the dropped letter is the first

blocks.note: fairer means paler in complexion or hair colour
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A comment that a picture frame looks lighter once a man has stopped sitting on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On top' tells you the fellow's letter goes from the head of the word, so FAIRER loses its first letter. An airer is a folding rack for drying laundry indoors, common in British homes.
explanation.definitionFit: An airer is a clothes-drying rack, a framework of rails on which washing hangs to dry.

clue.text: Gloomy warning about the end of Titanic, which spoiler provides

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that one is kept
about means around, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: feeling down is feeling low
the golfer's shouted warning
the final letter of Titanic

explanation.surface: A grim warning that someone is about to give away how the film Titanic ends.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Titanic a film and the spoiler a person revealing its plot; here the spoiler is the wing on a racing car. FORE is shouted on golf courses to warn of an incoming ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's rear spoiler deflects air upwards, which pushes the vehicle onto the road; that pressure is downforce.

clue.text: Leaders in election agree recount lest count's equal

indicators.note: leaders go at the front, so each word contributes only its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letters of these four words

explanation.surface: Election officials agree to a recount in case the tally comes out level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like part of the recount story, but it is the nobleman. The 's is short for is, so 'count's equal' reads 'a count is equal' in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is the British title ranked level with a continental count, so the two nobles are equivalents.

clue.text: Butterfly expert's first lesson, on removing wings?

definitions.text: Butterfly expert's first lesson, on removing wings?

blocks.note: surface reading: an insect collector learning to pin specimens
setter's reading: a swimmer who masters the butterfly stroke usually learned a simpler stroke first; and a butterfly without wings can only creep along

explanation.surface: A lepidopterist's first lesson, on pulling the wings off specimens.
explanation.walkthrough: Butterfly is a swimming stroke, so its expert is a swimmer, whose first lesson is usually freestyle; a wingless butterfly would also have to creep along on its front.
explanation.definitionFit: Freestyle is the basic swimming stroke most beginners learn before attempting the harder butterfly stroke.

clue.text: Term for rope after I fell in at sea?

definitions.text: Term for rope after I fell in at sea?

indicators.note: a term is an end point, so only the final letter is kept
after places one piece behind another, so the order is reversed from the clue
being at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are muddled

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of rope

explanation.surface: Someone who fell overboard asks what the rope thrown to them is called.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: the rope thrown to someone who has fallen into the sea is exactly this.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifeline is a rope thrown or attached to rescue a person in the water, the name for that rescue rope.

clue.text: Smart getting evacuated before widespread conflict

indicators.note: evacuating something empties it, so only its outer shell is kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of smart
rife means common and spreading everywhere

explanation.surface: A sensible decision to evacuate a town before a big war breaks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Widespread conflict' reads as one phrase meaning war, but the split comes between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Strife is bitter disagreement or fighting, so it is a direct synonym for conflict between people.

clue.text: Couple understand culture generally involves women

indicators.note: to involve is to wrap in or include, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: 'I see' means I understand
the arts: culture taken as a whole
W is the abbreviation for women

explanation.surface: An observation that a pair's grasp of culture tends to be shaped by women.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter for women slips in after the first letter of SEE, then THE ARTS follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple in love are sweethearts, the old affectionate term for two romantic partners.

clue.text: Jerry furious with Warne's last hair product

indicators.note: last points to the final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: a jerry is old slang for a chamber pot, as is po
mad means very angry
the final letter of Warne

explanation.surface: A man called Jerry is livid about the cricketer Shane Warne's latest hair treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: Jerry looks like a man's name or a German, but here it is the chamber pot, a po. Shane Warne was a famous Australian cricketer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomade is a scented grease or wax used to style hair and make it shine, so a grooming product.

clue.text: Line up in front of odd gallery full of Piaf's regrets

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
something full holds other things inside it

blocks.note: the first letter of odd
Edith Piaf sang 'Non, je ne regrette rien': she regretted nothing, rien in French
the Tate gallery in London

explanation.surface: Queuing outside a strange gallery stuffed with the French singer Piaf's regrets.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that Piaf's famous song says she regrets nothing, so her regrets are the French word for nothing. The Tate is London's best-known art gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: To orientate something is to position or align it in a particular direction, which is what lining up does.

clue.text: Geometrically divided illustration, clean Mondrian boxes?

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: the painter Piet Mondrian, known by his first name
to char is to do cleaning work; a char was a cleaning lady

explanation.surface: Mondrian's crisp boxes of colour are a geometrically divided picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxes' fits Mondrian's paintings of coloured rectangles, but it is a verb: the painter's first name encloses the cleaning word. Char is dated British for a cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: A pie chart is a diagram whose circle is cut into sectors, an illustration divided by geometry into slices.

clue.text: Pantomime character in theatre regularly: large horse (back end missing)

indicators.note: regular means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept
the back end of a word is its last letter, and missing means it is dropped

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of theatre
L is the abbreviation for large
equine means of or like a horse

explanation.surface: A panto horse in a theatre, with the rear half missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back end missing' evokes a pantomime horse missing the actor in its hind legs, but it only trims a letter. Pantomime is a British Christmas stage show.
explanation.definitionFit: Harlequin is the masked, diamond-costumed clown of traditional pantomime and Italian commedia, a stock role in those shows.

clue.text: Trouble for miners made redundant by a politician

blocks.note: sacked from a job
taken as written
a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Pit closures by a government minister cause hardship in mining communities.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls British pit closures, making 'trouble' sound political; it is the gas danger underground.
explanation.definitionFit: Firedamp is methane gas found in coal mines, which can explode and so poses a deadly hazard to workers underground.

clue.text: Year dot starts hot

blocks.note: to pepper is to dot or sprinkle all over
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: The year dot, the very beginning of time, began scorching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Year dot' is a British phrase for the distant past, but the two words split: 'dot starts' puts its piece first, with the year's letter after.
explanation.definitionFit: Peppery food is spicy and pungent, so it tastes hot in the sense of fiery seasoning.

clue.text: Sheep and grass around bull's location

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the order runs backwards

blocks.note: a teg is a sheep in its second year
to grass or rat is to inform on someone

explanation.surface: Sheep and grass surround a bull in a farm field.
explanation.walkthrough: The farmyard makes the bull an animal; it is the bullseye at the centre of a dartboard. To grass is British slang for informing to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: The bull, or bullseye, is the centre ring of a dartboard or archery target, so that is where it sits.

clue.text: Man due for a makeover left messy

definitions.note: past participle phrase; unmade is the adjective it describes, as in a bed left unmade

indicators.note: a makeover remodels something, so these letters are rearranged into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A scruffy man who needs a style makeover has been left looking untidy.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes a person the messy one; the answer describes a bed nobody has tidied.
explanation.definitionFit: An unmade bed is one left untidy, with covers not straightened after sleeping in it.

clue.text: House changes with Victor's departure

indicators.note: on departure something leaves, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: to vary is to change
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A household changes after Victor moves out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House' looks like a home, but astrologers divide the zodiac into houses, and each sign rules one.
explanation.definitionFit: Aries, the ram, is the first sign of the zodiac and is linked with the first astrological house.

clue.text: Excuse groom taking time before church

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: to preen is to groom oneself
T is the abbreviation for time
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A bridegroom's excuse for spending so long before the wedding service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' looks like the man getting married; it is the verb for smartening up.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretence is a false reason given to hide the real one, which is what a flimsy excuse amounts to.

clue.text: Governing principles Conservative put differently

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
to redo something is to do it again in another way

explanation.surface: A Tory restating the party's ruling principles in new words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put differently' sounds like a signal to rearrange letters, but it is a plain synonym for doing over.
explanation.definitionFit: A credo is a statement of beliefs that guides someone's actions, a personal creed or set of rules to live by.

clue.text: What mum might put on boy that is blind

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
i.e. is the abbreviation for 'that is'
'eff and blind' is British slang for swearing, so to blind is to curse

explanation.surface: A mother dressing her son, who cannot see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blind' looks like an adjective for the boy, but it is the verb from the British phrase 'effing and blinding', meaning cursing.
explanation.definitionFit: Ladieswear is the shop term for women's clothing, the kind of garments a mother would dress in.

clue.text: Body on a large bed whose attitude is accommodating

indicators.note: to accommodate is to house, so the phrase holds the letters inside it

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone lying on a big bed with a very obliging manner.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'body on a large bed' sounds like a person in bed; it is a body of water lying on the seabed.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea is a large body of salt water, and it lies over the floor of the ocean, called its bed.

clue.text: Socialist in the Soviet Union going out for 27?

definitions.text: Socialist in the Soviet Union going out for 27?

indicators.note: one thing going out to make room for another is a swap of one letter for another

blocks.note: the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
S is the abbreviation for socialist
the answer to 27 is the drug ecstasy, known as E

explanation.surface: A Soviet socialist heading out for an evening of bliss.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the two S's in USSR is swapped for E, the drug's slang name. Read whole, the clue is also the definition: someone out to get ecstasy.
explanation.definitionFit: A user is someone who takes drugs, and the clue pictures a person going out to find ecstasy.

clue.text: Old lover to meet up with sounds like bliss

indicators.note: this says plainly that the spoken form, not the spelling, gives the answer

blocks.clueFragment: Old lover to meet up with
blocks.note: an old lover is an ex; to meet up with someone is to see them

explanation.surface: Arranging to meet a former partner again feels wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, 'ex to see' runs together into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecstasy is overwhelming joy or rapture, so it is a direct synonym for a state of complete happiness.

clue.text: NATO manoeuvres occupying ship in Atlantic port

indicators.note: military manoeuvres move units around, so the letters are rearranged
to occupy is to sit inside, so one piece goes within another
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: SS stands for steamship
taken as written

explanation.surface: NATO naval exercises in a harbour on the Atlantic coast.
explanation.walkthrough: Santos is a major Brazilian port on the Atlantic, Pelé's old football club's home.
explanation.definitionFit: Santos lies on Brazil's southeastern coast and handles much of the country's shipping, a harbour on the Atlantic Ocean.
